content: I recall seeing some thread analyzing quality of the formalizations but it has apparently disappeared ... (I didn't save it)

I find it very odd that the "pinnacle" prize is for formalization of 7 problems which just happen to be the Clay problems, although nowhere does this coincidence seem to be mentioned (maybe I missed it).

On vibes, the website does not inspire confidence.

On the plus side, some data on how they make decisions appears to be public in this repo https://github.com/TheJustinSunPrize/awards
I submitted one of my formalizations, I'll update with how the process goes.

5 messages were moved here from #Funding opportunities > The Justin Sun Prize by Kim Morrison.

Hi folks, another update on the Justin Sun Prize: https://www.theblock.co/sponsored/2026-10-05-justin-sun-prizes-new-round-honors-human-ai-collaboration-on-erdos-problems-417743

We've awarded prizes for work done on Erdős Problems 650, 369, 457, 469, 1044, and 1196.

You can see more details in the press release above or on this Github repo: https://github.com/TheJustinSunPrize/awards

@JustinSunPrize, in the last few days, the erdos problems website underwent significant changes since

The situation as it stands muddies the waters, promotes a gamified glory-seeking attitude, and gives the wrong impression that the value of these questions ends as soon as someone posts a formal proof of their truth value. This is not true (regardless of whether this proof was human or AI generated).

For example, the "open" and "solved" tags were removed due to this.

As you are explicitly mentioning Erdos problems, have you incorporated/considered any of those considerations? In particular as due to the monetary nature of the prize.

@JustinSunPrize I've only submitted one formalization, which has sat around with no review for over 2 weeks. I'm sure that's because there are users creating hundreds of slop PRs with a formalization that doesn't actually solve the problem, or try to take credit for other formalizations. I would recommend investing in a bot that can review and tag submissions as likely credible or does not meet standards, it's going to be difficult to tackle the backlog without some kind of prioritization and automation like that. Although you can easily predict which users are throwing up slop, they usually have more than 5 open PRs and they're constantly closing and reopening them because they're not using competent AI for even making the submission.

I would additionally recommend, if you look at lean-eval, they lock down the types of the theorem that the problem represents to verified mathlib definitions of the problem itself, which can be enforced in a Challenge/Solution with comparator check. If each problem had one of those locked down, it would make it much easier to reject slop because their fully machine checked sorry free formalizations would have to solve the actual problem or use axioms and conditionals to get around it.
